cwd_src.description: Present only when the host never declared a logical working directory, so cwd is the process's physical directory rather than the path the user sees. Absent when the host declared it.

origin.description: How the shell was invoked (interactive REPL, -c, script file, stdin script)

origin_src.description: Present only when the host never declared how the shell was invoked, so origin fell back to unknown. Absent when declared.

dialect.description: Which dialect executed the line. It separates two things `source` would otherwise conflate: who wrote the record (the tool / process name) and the dialect of the pane; the process and the dialect can move independently. Optional, and stays optional: older records do not carry it, and the schema of an append-only ledger must validate every line ever written. Absence means the producer did not know the dialect, not that there was none: a record built without hsh's emitter carries none. Not a rename of `source`, and a consumer must not derive either field from the other: 'bash' and 'sh' share the source 'hsh-bash'. A closed enum, like origin's and actor_kind's: a new dialect on the producer side is added here in the same change, so the ledger never holds a value its dictionary cannot spell.

actor.description: Who ran it (high-cardinality identity). An administrator-set name (AUDIT_ACTOR) wins; then an agent that names itself in the environment (AI_AGENT, CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT, normalised to its leading segment, e.g. claude-code); then $USER/$LOGNAME; else 'unknown'. The agent comes before the OS user so that an agent's work is not filed under the human's name.

actor_kind.description: Low-cardinality classification of actor for aggregation. A host setting it per pane wins; then 'agent' if an agent names itself in the environment; then 'ci' if $CI is truthy; else the field is absent. Every value is a claim someone makes. 'human' is retired and no longer emitted: it was inferred from an interactive origin (a TTY, not a person), which is false under a persistent PTY. It stays in the enum only so that older records validate; do not emit it. Older records may also carry 'unknown', meaning nobody claimed it. Who was actually present is carried by observers instead (attach:* peer credentials, uid/auid on session:start).

modified.description: Legacy spelling of `ts`, no longer emitted or required. Kept declared because archived records carry it. See spec/PROTOCOL_v1.md 2.05.

id.description: Correlation id for this execution. Emitted on cmd:run and returned on cmd:end, so the pair can be matched, which makes 'a run with no end' (the shell was killed mid-command) visible. Format is {pid:x}-{nanos:x}: unique within one machine's journal, not a global identifier. Optional: older records have none, and a consumer must not read its absence as 'unfinished'.

on_behalf_of.description: The human whose environment an agent was running in (the OS user). Present only when actor_kind is 'agent': the actor is then the agent's name, and this keeps the person ('an agent, in alice's checkout').

body_bytes.description: Size of the script body, for an invocation whose cmd does not hold the text itself. Two origins have one, for different reasons: 'stdin' because the body evaporates (cmd holds the fixed marker '(stdin script)'), and 'script' because the body persists but is editable (the path names a file, not the program that ran under it). 'command' (-c) has neither: its cmd already is the body. Older records may carry neither, so absence is not evidence that a file was unchanged.

body_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the script body, lower-case hex. The body itself is never stored: a copy held elsewhere matches against this, as does a seal chain using the same hash. Scope: this covers the one file the cmd names and nothing it pulled in. A file it sourced into the same process is not included, so a matching hash means 'this text is unchanged', not 'the same program ran'. A child process running another script keeps its own record with its own digest; what a binary or an exec'd program did is outside a shell's sight. Bodies sourced into the same process are a known gap: a consumer should treat their absence as such, not as a settled contract.

body_preview.description: First N bytes of the body, cut back to a UTF-8 boundary. Opt-in only (HSH_JOURNAL_STDIN_PREVIEW=<N>) and absent by default: a heredoc often carries a token, and hash matching does not need the text. A consumer must not assume it is present, or that it is the whole body.

ts.description: When the event happened, on the producer's clock. RFC 3339. `ts` is the canonical name (spec/PROTOCOL_v1.md 2.05). Older records may carry `modified` (or `timestamp`) instead, so a consumer reading archived records falls back `ts ?? modified ?? timestamp`.

sourced.description: Every file whose body the shell read and ran through source / . during this command, nested sources included, in the order first read; the same (path, body_sha256) appears once. Absent when nothing was sourced. Startup files and PROMPT_COMMAND run outside the command and are not listed; on unix, sources inside forked children (subshells, command substitution) are not listed either.

body_sha256.description: sha256 of the body as it was run (not re-read)

sourced_omitted.description: How many more sourced bodies there were beyond the 64 listed in sourced. Absent when none were left out.

notification:published.description: A system notification is published and active (a delivery service -> desktop apps)

link:found.description: A link discovered while scouting a page (Marrow scout)

chunk:existing.description: A content section discovered during a read (Marrow read; web analogue of file:existing). Snapshot, not a delta. chunk_id is provisional (anchor + content hash) on a bare read and becomes durable once aligned under monitoring.

chunk:modified.description: A content section changed since last seen (Marrow change tracking; analogue of file:modified)

chunk:moved.description: A content section moved position since last seen (Marrow change tracking)

chunk:removed.description: A content section was removed since last seen (Marrow change tracking; analogue of file:deleted)

diff:completed.description: Summary of a change-tracking diff run (Marrow)

media:mark.description: A moment in a media file was marked while watching (timestamped observation)

time_s.description: Playback position in seconds. The machine axis — timecode is a projection of this

timecode.description: Human-readable position: H:MM:SS past the hour, else MM:SS (e.g. 1:20:27)

media_title.description: Title reported by the player (mpv media-title), falling back to the file name

media_path.description: Path or URL of the media being played

note.description: What the watcher observed at this moment. Absent for a bare mark

session:start.description: A shell session began — one process, one login (hsh-bash journal)

sid.description: Session id, fixed for the process. Every cmd/env/alias record from this shell carries it, so the session is the spine the rest hangs from. Format {pid:x}-{nanos:x} — unique on one machine's journal, not globally.

uid.description: getuid() — who is running now. Differs from auid after su/sudo, and that difference is the point.

auid.description: Linux loginuid: who logged in. The kernel sets it at login and refuses to let it be reset, so it survives su/sudo. uid=0 with auid=1000 means 'user 1000 logged in and became root' — the line getuid() alone cannot say. Absent where the OS does not provide it.

login.description: Login name from the OS, not from the environment.

tty.description: Controlling terminal, when there is one.

from.description: Peer address of the ssh connection this session came in on, when it did. Read from the environment sshd sets, so it is an observation of what sshd reported — present only for remote logins.

actor_src.description: Where the actor string on this session's records came from, mirroring the resolution order: explicit (a host set it per pane), audit_actor (AUDIT_ACTOR — the name an administrator sets), agent (a tool's self-declaration: AI_AGENT, CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT), user / logname (the OS login name), unknown. Older records may carry hsh_actor (the retired HSH_ACTOR). This separates a claim from an observation: a caller declaring a name reads audit_actor, while a plain login reads user — so an impersonation marks itself.

ver.description: Release version of the shell that wrote this.

build.description: Git short hash of the source it was built from, '-dirty' when the tree had uncommitted changes, 'unknown' when git could not answer. A version alone cannot identify a deployment: several commits can ship under one version.

argod_session.description: The join key under the daemon's former name: older records carry this instead of berthd_session. The shell still reads the old environment variable ARGOD_SESSION as a fallback, but writes berthd_session.

berthd_session.description: The berthd session this shell runs under — the value the child sees in BERTHD_SESSION (ARGOD_SESSION is read as a fallback). The join key to berthd's attach records: under berthd this shell's actor stops meaning 'who is typing', and who attached is in those records, keyed by this.

from_port.description: Client port of the ssh connection: the second field of SSH_CONNECTION (or SSH_CLIENT), from the same variable as from. With host, from and the time it joins the line sshd writes by default ('Accepted publickey ... from <ip> port <n>'), which names the key used — no sshd configuration needed.

auth_src.description: Where the authentication observation came from, written whenever the session came over ssh: ssh_user_auth (the file sshd writes when ExposeAuthInfo is on), unset (the server does not expose it — not 'no key was used'), unreadable (the path was set but could not be read). Always written for an ssh session, like identity_src, so 'the server said nothing' and 'no key was used' stay apart.

auth.description: The authentication methods the server observed, one element per method in the order sshd recorded them (multi-factor gives more than one). key is the base64 public key exactly as sshd wrote it — the same spelling as authorized_keys, so it matches with grep -F; no fingerprint is derived (ssh-keygen -lf computes one, and from_port joins the sshd log line that carries it). Only publickey carries key_type and key. Present only where the server exposes it; auth_src says why when it is absent. The producer does not classify which key belongs to an agent. The policy keeps the zero-configuration log join open as the alternative.

ancestry.description: This process (element 0) and its parents at session start — at most 8, never pid 1. Names are comm only; arguments are never recorded. Tells which tool the shell started under (claude, codex, ...) with no configuration; the producer does not classify. Over ssh the chain includes sshd's [priv] process, whose pid is the one sshd logs. Linux and macOS only; elsewhere absent, and ancestry_src says why.

ancestry_src.description: Where ancestry came from and why it stopped: proc / proc_pidinfo / toolhelp (reached below pid 1; on Windows the walk normally ends :vanished instead, because the OS does not reparent and an exited parent's pid is not in the snapshot), ...:depth_limit (cut at 8), ...:vanished (a parent was gone — ESRCH), ...:denied (a parent was there but refused — EPERM, e.g. /proc mounted with hidepid; never produced on Windows), ...:unreadable (the read failed for another reason, or a line could not be parsed), unavailable:... (this process itself could not be read), unimplemented:ios / unimplemented:android / unimplemented:ancestry. Always written, like identity_src. A permission failure is never reported as a disappearance.

os_sessionid.description: Audit session id of the login this shell runs in (Linux /proc/self/sessionid, macOS BSM ai_asid). Separate from the shell's own sid; it joins auditd / journald and berthd's peer_session. Read it with identity_src.

identity_src.description: Which mechanism answered uid / auid / os_sessionid, or why none could (e.g. loginuid on Linux, token_user on Windows). Always written: without it a missing auid reads the same whether the platform cannot answer or an older binary did not record it.

user_sid.description: Windows: the process's user SID — the Windows spelling of 'which user', where there is no uid.

lc_ctype.description: The LC_CTYPE the environment requested at start (LC_ALL > LC_CTYPE > LANG, empty treated as unset). A request at one point in time: a later export applies from the next command, so reconstructing the effective value needs the env records that follow.

lc_ctype_src.description: Which variable lc_ctype came from (LC_ALL, LC_CTYPE or LANG).

sid.description: Matches the session:start that opened it.

how.description: How it ended: 'clean' for exit or EOF, 'hangup' for a dropped connection. Emitted once per process — whichever path reaches it first wins — so start and end stay one to one.

attach:start.description: A client attached to a persistent session (berthd; named argod in older records). Identity belongs to the attachment, not the process: the daemon outlives any one client, a shell outlives any one attachment, and someone else can attach later, so a shell, which resolves its actor once at startup, cannot say who is typing now. The required fields are the ones every record carries; the session key's name changed with the daemon's name, so it is not among them.

berthd_session.description: The session attached to, and the join key to the shell's own ledger: a shell running under berthd writes the same value in session:start (berthd_session), and its child sees it in BERTHD_SESSION. Older records carry argod_session instead.

argod_session.description: The same key under the daemon's former name (argod). Older records carry this instead of berthd_session; no producer writes it any more.

name.description: Human-facing name of the session (the handle people type); the id is an internal key.

peer_uid.description: uid of the connecting client, from the unix socket's peer credentials. Observed, not claimed: the kernel answers. Absent where the OS does not answer. Read it beside actor: disagreement between the two is the interesting case; where a person and their agents share one uid, this field alone cannot separate them.

peer_pid.description: pid of the connecting client, same source. Absent where the OS does not answer.

peer_session.description: The connecting client's login or service compartment. Its meaning depends on the platform, so read it with peer_identity_src: on Linux the audit session id (/proc/<pid>/sessionid), on macOS the BSM audit session id from LOCAL_PEERTOKEN, on Windows the Terminal Services session id (0 = a service, i.e. ssh; 1 and above = an interactive login). On Linux and macOS it joins hsh's os_sessionid, which is how an ssh hop becomes a chain.

peer_identity_src.description: How the peer fields were obtained, or why they could not be (e.g. so_peercred+proc_sessionid, so_peercred+local_peertoken:unset, unavailable:so_peercred). Always written: without it an empty peer field reads the same whether the platform cannot answer or an older daemon did not record it.

peer_auid.description: The connecting client's audit user id: who logged in first; it survives sudo. Linux: /proc/<pid>/loginuid; macOS: the LOCAL_PEERTOKEN audit token. Absent when unset (the 4294967295 sentinel) and on Windows, which has no such id. Matches auid on hsh's session:start.

peer_ancestry.description: The attaching process and its parents, read at the moment of attachment: element 0 is the client itself, then its parent, and so on, at most 8, never pid 1. Names are comm only; arguments are never recorded (they can carry secrets). A reader can tell which tool attached (claude, codex, ...) without any configuration; the producer does not classify. Over ssh the chain includes sshd's [priv] process, whose pid is the one sshd writes in its log ('Accepted publickey ... sshd[<pid>]'), so the key used can be joined without changing sshd's configuration. The end record repeats the start's value rather than re-reading it.

peer_ancestry_src.description: Where the chain came from and why it stopped: proc / proc_pidinfo / toolhelp (reached below pid 1; on Windows the walk normally ends :vanished instead, because the OS does not reparent and an exited parent's pid is not in the snapshot), ...:depth_limit (cut at 8), ...:vanished (a parent was gone, ESRCH), ...:denied (a parent was there but refused, EPERM; not produced on Windows, where the snapshot does not open processes), ...:unreadable (the read failed for another reason, or a line could not be parsed), unavailable:proc / unavailable:proc_pidinfo / unavailable:toolhelp (the client itself could not be read), unavailable:peer_pid (no pid to start from). Always written, for the same reason as peer_identity_src. A permission failure is never reported as a disappearance.

daemon_session.description: The compartment the daemon itself is in (same mechanism as peer_session). When a child shell's os_sessionid equals this, the number describes where berthd was started, not the login that attached.

daemon_session_src.description: How daemon_session was obtained, or why not. Always written.

actor.description: The name the attaching client claimed for itself (claude-code, deploy-bot, ...), carried on the attach request. Unverified by construction: the ledger records the claim as a claim, next to the kernel's observation, and leaves believing to the reader. Absent means nobody claimed anything; the daemon does not fill it in from the OS user name, which is already in peer_uid. Only a name is carried, never a category. Resolution on the client: AUDIT_ACTOR, then the traces AI_AGENT and CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT. Spelled like the shell's own ledger, so the two can be joined on berthd_session without translating the column; older records spell it claimed_actor.

claimed_actor.description: Older spelling of actor; no producer writes it any more. The name the attaching client claimed for itself (claude-code, deploy-bot, ...), carried on the attach request. Unverified by construction: the ledger records the claim as a claim, next to the kernel's observation, and leaves believing to the reader. Absent means nobody claimed anything; the daemon does not fill it in from the OS user name, which is already in peer_uid. Only a name is carried, never a category.

actor_src.description: Where the claimed name came from on the client. The shipped clients (berth, argotty) send one of: audit_actor (the environment set AUDIT_ACTOR, the name an administrator sets); agent (a self-declaration a tool leaves in the environment: AI_AGENT, CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT). Older records may carry hsh_actor (the retired HSH_ACTOR variable). Not a closed list: it is part of the client's claim and recorded as received, not corrected. Absent when no name was claimed. Older records spell it claimed_actor_src.

claimed_actor_src.description: Older spelling of actor_src; no producer writes it any more. Where the claimed name came from on the client. The shipped clients (berth, argotty) send one of: audit_actor (the environment set AUDIT_ACTOR, the name an administrator sets); agent (a self-declaration a tool leaves in the environment: AI_AGENT, CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT). Older records may carry hsh_actor (the retired HSH_ACTOR variable). Not a closed list: it is part of the client's claim and recorded as received, not corrected. Absent when no name was claimed.

client.description: What the client said it is in its Hello: the GUI writes 'argotty', the CLI 'berth/<version> (<build>)'. Unverified (a claim, like actor), but on Windows, where there is no uid, it can be the only hint of what connected. Written as received, not normalised. Spelled as on the wire; older records spell it claimed_client.

claimed_client.description: Older spelling of client; no producer writes it any more. What the client said it is in its Hello: the GUI writes 'argotty', the CLI 'berth/<version> (<build>)'. Unverified (a claim, like actor), but on Windows, where there is no uid, it can be the only hint of what connected. Written as received, not normalised.

read_only.description: Whether this was a watch-only attachment (berth attach -r): it received the output, but its keystrokes and resizes were dropped, and it did not replace the operator. Any number can be attached beside the one operator. Older records do not carry it; they are all operators.

ver.description: Release version of the daemon that wrote this.

build.description: Git short hash of the daemon's source. Client and daemon are deployed separately, so they drift routinely.

attach:end.description: A client's attachment to a persistent session ended (berthd; named argod in older records). Carries the same identity fields as the start record, repeated rather than re-read.

name.description: Human-facing name of the session (the handle people type); the id is an internal key.

peer_uid.description: uid of the connecting client, from the unix socket's peer credentials. Observed, not claimed: the kernel answers. Absent where the OS does not answer. peer_pid.description: pid of the connecting client, same source. Absent where the OS does not answer.

peer_session.description: The connecting client's login or service compartment. peer_ancestry.description: The attaching process and its parents, read at the moment of attachment: element 0 is the client itself, then its parent, and so on, at most 8, never pid 1. Over ssh the chain includes sshd's [priv] process, whose pid is the one sshd writes in its log ('Accepted publickey ... sshd[<pid>]'), so the key used can be joined without changing sshd's configuration. The end record repeats the start's value rather than re-reading it.

peer_ancestry_src.description: Where the chain came from and why it stopped: proc / proc_pidinfo / toolhelp (reached below pid 1; on Windows the walk normally ends :vanished instead, because the OS does not reparent and an exited parent's pid is not in the snapshot), ...:depth_limit (cut at 8), ...:vanished (a parent was gone, ESRCH), ...:denied (a parent was there but refused, EPERM; not produced on Windows, where the snapshot does not open processes), ...:unreadable (the read failed for another reason, or a line could not be parsed), unavailable:proc / unavailable:proc_pidinfo / unavailable:toolhelp (the client itself could not be read), unavailable:peer_pid (no pid to start from). daemon_session_src.description: How daemon_session was obtained, or why not. Always written.

env:set.description: A variable was assigned or exported (hsh journal). Recorded only when origin is 'interactive': a typed assignment is an act, while one inside a script or -c is part of an invocation whose own cmd record already exists, so a consumer must not read the absence of these records as 'the script changed nothing'. Startup rc files are sourced interactively, so a shell's opening aliases and exports appear too. Opt out with HSH_LOG_ENV=0. The value is whatever was assigned: an interactively exported credential is recorded verbatim. The one exception is `read -s`: the person typing declared that the value must not be shown, so the producer omits `value` entirely and says so in `value_withheld`. This is not redaction (nothing is scanned or guessed); it fires only on that explicit declaration. A consumer must therefore treat a missing `value` as 'withheld', not as 'empty'.

value.description: The value after the change. Explicitly null on unset (this record type writes null rather than omitting the field, unlike session:start).

value_withheld.description: Present only when the producer deliberately did not store the value; names the reason. hsh writes "read-s" for an interactive `read -s`. When this is present, `value` is absent (not null) — null means 'unset' on this record type, which is a different fact.

body_bytes.description: Size of the body in bytes, as `wc -c` counts it.

flux:rewrite.description: hsh's Flux mode (HSH_FLUX) rewrote a pipeline before running it (hsh journal). It records the shell's own act of rewriting, not the data the inserted stages emitted. The cmd record keeps the line as typed; this record puts the typed and the effective shapes side by side, because their difference is itself the fact. typed.description: The pipeline before the rewrite, rendered back from the parsed AST — whitespace is normalised, so it is not byte-for-byte what was typed. The literal typed line is the `cmd` of the cmd:run named by cmd_id.

effective.description: The pipeline that actually ran, rendered the same way, with the inserted stages in place and the original `!` restored.

inserted.description: The stages the shell inserted, in pipeline order (e.g. ["sig --no-journal", "unsig"]).

origin_src.description: Present only when the host never declared how the shell was invoked, so origin fell back to unknown: the value is undeclared. Absent when declared.

actor.description: Who ran it (high-cardinality identity). The agent comes before the OS user so that an agent's work is not filed under a person's name. Older records may carry a name taken from $HSH_ACTOR.

vault:overwrite.description: A note was written whole (vault journal). Every write inside the vault app passes one gate (vault_mutate), which is what makes this stream complete for writes it made — writes from outside the gate arrive later as vault:reconcile.

vault.description: Absolute path of the vault root, so several vaults on one machine stay apart.

vault_id.description: The vault's identity (32 lowercase hex), when one has been issued — only connecting to sync issues it, so a local-only vault has none. It lets history survive the vault being moved; path alone cannot, and records without it are dropped from the comparison after a move. Older records lack it.

path.description: Path of the note, relative to the vault root.

actor.description: Who the write is filed under. Low-cardinality by design: the vault app classifies rather than naming a person, because the name it could print is whatever the caller sent. Only the first three can be claimed by a caller -- 'sync', 'external', 'app' and 'unnamed' name what the vault app did or concluded, and an edge refuses them as claims, so a caller cannot file its own write as something the patrol found. 'unnamed' is a keyholder that came through the gate and named nobody; older records file that case as 'external'. Read together with actor_src, which says whether anybody claimed it at all.

actor_id.description: Free-form identifier beside actor, when the caller supplied one or the code knew it (an agent's client name, a plugin id, 'scaffold'). Absent means nobody named anything, not that the actor was anonymous by policy.

actor_src.description: Where the actor value came from — the same question session:start answers with its actor_src, spelled for the vault app's doors because the mechanisms differ. 'api' is a claim in an HTTP body (the gate is one shared key, so a holder can name anyone); 'api_default' is an HTTP caller that named nothing, where the edge wrote actor=external — without this value that record would be indistinguishable from a change the patrol found. 'ipc'/'ipc_default' are the Tauri invoke door, the latter being a person saving in the editor: a genuine actor=human only ever arrives this way, so actor=human with actor_src=api means the human-only path was bypassed. 'internal' is the vault app's own code, first-hand. 'inferred' is the patrol's conclusion from a hash diff, where no actor was observed at all. Absent on records from binaries that predate the field; absence means that, not 'unknown provenance'.

sha256.description: SHA-256 of the fragment that was written, lower-case hex. Absent for ops that write no content.

result_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the whole file after the write. This is what makes the ledger replayable from the journal alone, which is how the patrol knows what it should be seeing. Absent for ops that leave no file (delete, mkdir, a directory copy).

reason.description: What the scan concluded. 'changed' and 'deleted' are measured against the ledger. result_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the file as found. Absent when the reason is deleted.

prev_sha256.description: The hash the ledger last knew, kept as a headstone for a deletion and as the handle for an undelete. Absent when there was nothing to compare against.

ts.description: When the record was written. Older records from some producers spell it `modified`, so a consumer reading archived records handles both. For reconcile this is when the change was *noticed*, which is not when it happened.

vault:patrol.description: A patrol round finished, including a quiet one (vault journal). stall:bursted.description: One burst of Marrow's deep reads fired at a single fixture to reproduce a load-correlated stall. Sibling of stall:sampled, kept separate: the hourly sampler applies no load and never varies the image, so its denominator cannot say which deploy made stalls stop. Stored, so it carries ts.

ts.description: RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. When the burst finished, by the producer's clock (§2.05). Present because this signal is stored in a ledger rather than streamed.

worker.description: Base URL of the worker that was shot. May be a shadow container on a spare port, not production.

image.description: Which build was shot — the container's image reference, or the baked git commit when the worker names one. null means it could not be established, which makes the burst useless for comparing builds; the tool exits 2 rather than calling that a measurement.

image_from.description: Whose answer 'image' is: 'health' is the worker naming its own baked commit, 'container' is docker inspect on the host. Not the same fact — an image tag can be retagged, a baked commit cannot.

bun.description: The Bun version inside that build, when the worker names it. null means the build does not report its runtime in /health — not that the version is unknowable (docker run --entrypoint bun can still read it).

fixture.description: Which fixture every shot in this burst was aimed at. One fixture per burst: mixing pages inside a burst mixes denominators.

fixture_sha.description: The denominator's real identity: the git blob hash of the fixture bytes actually served. A fixture's name alone does not name a workload, because its content can change.

shots.description: How many requests this burst made.

concurrency.description: How many were in flight at once. 1 means sequential. Part of the denominator: the failure being chased is load-correlated, so a rate without this number cannot be compared.

stalled.description: How many shots the worker itself reported as a browser stall (crawl-timeout).

stalled_at.description: Which pipeline stage each stall was in flight at, when the stage clock could name one. Builds without a stage clock leave it empty, so an empty list is not the same fact as 'no stage'.

no_response.description: How many shots the tool itself cut off at its own deadline. Not the same fact as stalled — here the worker said nothing.

broken.description: How many shots failed for any other reason (a real red).

elapsed_ms_median.description: Median wall time of the shots that answered. null when none did.

elapsed_ms_max.description: Slowest shot that answered. Read next to the worker's crawl budget: it says whether the burst was near the edge or nowhere near it.

worker_uptime_sec.description: How long the worker had been running continuously. null means it could not be measured — not zero.

uptime_from.description: Whose age worker_uptime_sec is: 'health' is the process, 'container' is docker inspect StartedAt. Not the same quantity.

label.description: Free note from whoever fired it (which arm of the experiment this is). Never used to group rates — that is what image and fixture_sha are for.

stall:sampled.description: One run of Marrow's deploy rig measuring the deep-stall rate: a fixed set of fixtures shot once each, with how many stalled. Stored, so it carries ts.

ts.description: RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. When the run finished, by the producer's clock (§2.05). Present because this signal is stored in a ledger rather than streamed — a live receiver knows "now", a file does not.

worker.description: Base URL of the worker that was shot.

fixtures.description: The denominator: which fixtures this run shot. Rates must be split by this set — when the set changes, mixing runs turns 'the extractor improved' and 'a fixture was added' into the same number.

shots.description: How many requests this run made (len(fixtures), one each).

stalled.description: How many shots the worker itself reported as a browser stall (crawl-timeout).

stalled_at.description: Which pipeline stage each stall was in flight at, when the stage clock could name one.

no_response.description: How many shots the rig itself cut off at its own deadline. Not the same fact as stalled — here the worker said nothing, so a stall and a regression cannot be told apart from this run alone.

broken.description: How many shots failed for any other reason (a real red).

worker_uptime_sec.description: How long the worker had been running continuously. null means it could not be measured — not zero.

uptime_from.description: Whose age worker_uptime_sec is: 'health' is the process (the worker said so), 'container' is the container (docker inspect StartedAt). Not the same quantity; absent means the record predates the field, which must not be read as 'health'.

mode.description: Which rig mode fired this run. Absent means the run predates the field — a third state, not "sample".

warmup:surveyed.description: One round of Marrow's survey measuring whether the humanoid warmup still gets past bot walls. Stored, so it carries ts.

ts.description: RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. When the run finished, by the producer's clock (§2.05). Present because this signal is stored in a ledger rather than streamed — a live receiver knows "now", a file does not.

pages.description: Which live pages this round visited.

walls.description: Per warmup variant (none/sleep/scroll/full), how many pages answered with a bot wall.

threw.description: Per warmup variant, how many pages threw. Counted next to walls because a JS challenge navigates away before innerText is read — a wall shows up here.

rescued_by_full.description: The number to read: pages lost with the shipped warmup minus pages lost with the full one. A difference, not a rate — a target that got stricter hits both arms equally and cancels.

lost_by.description: How "lost" was counted for this round (e.g. wall+threw).

stream:data.description: One line of text a data-plane stage carried, wrapped as a record (hsh's sig, and the bundled fetch). source is the stage (sig, fetch), not the process.

line.description: The line as it arrived, without its line ending.

path.description: What was observed, when the stage observed something (fetch: the URL it fetched; sig: the line itself, when it names a file or directory that exists, relative to cwd). Absent when nothing was observed.

cwd.description: Where the stage stood (sig: the working directory). Absent for fetch. Older records spell it path.

line:matched.description: One line of a file matched a pattern (rheon-grep). The plain form is grep -rn's path:line:text. Older records may carry match:found.

text.description: The line as it is in the file, without its line ending (not trimmed).

context.description: Surrounding lines, `  N| text`; the match itself is `> N| text`.

file:matched.description: A file whose path fuzzily matched a query (rheon-find). Older records may carry match:found.

text.description: The file name (last component) -- not a line of content.

score.description: Fuzzy match score; results come highest first.

file:read.description: A file read within a token budget (rheon-read). Older records may carry ctx:read.

content.description: The text read (cut at the budget when truncated).

next_offset.description: Where to continue a cut read.

start_line.description: Read by line range (--lines): the first line shown, 1-based.

end_line.description: The last line shown in full; start_line - 1 when not even the first line fit the budget.

next_line.description: When a line-range read was cut by the budget: the line to continue from (--lines <next_line>:).

file:written.description: rheon-write replaced the whole file (overwrite). type is the subject (the file); event is what happened to it. Older records may carry write:written.

file:appended.description: rheon-write appended to the file. type is the subject (the file); event is what happened to it. Older records may carry write:appended.

file:replaced.description: rheon-write replaced a range of lines. type is the subject (the file); event is what happened to it. Older records may carry write:replaced.

file:moved.description: rheon-write moved the file (dest says where). type is the subject (the file); event is what happened to it. Older records may carry write:moved.

entry:observed.description: One entry of a directory listing (rheon-ls), the records version of ls. The plain form is name. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

hidden.description: dot name on unix; the hidden attribute on Windows

usage:observed.description: Disk usage of a directory, totals of everything under it (rheon-du), the records version of du. Sorted by path. The plain form is du -B1's disk<TAB>path. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

partial.description: something under it could not be read

count:observed.description: Counts for one input (rheon-wc), the records version of wc. Fields not asked for (-l -w -c -m -L) are left out, not null; null means could not count. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

path.description: null for text read from stdin

chars.description: null when the content is not UTF-8

identity:observed.description: Who the process runs as (rheon-id), the records version of id. On Windows uid / gid are null and sid / domain carry the identity. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

group:observed.description: One group the process belongs to (rheon-id); one record per group, like id -Gn one per line. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

process:observed.description: One process (rheon-proc). A value the platform does not give is null, never 0 or a guess: macOS answers zeros for another user's process, so threads / rss_kb / cpu_time_s are null there rather than look idle.

name.description: full name (ps -o comm cuts it at 15)

host:observed.description: The machine (rheon-proc): name, OS, kernel release, architecture, boot time. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

checksum:observed.description: The digest of one file (rheon-sum), the records version of sha256sum / md5sum. Named checksum because digest belongs to rheon-digest. The plain form is sha256sum's: digest, two spaces, path. A value the platform does not have is null, never 0 or a guess.

load:observed.description: Load average and uptime (rheon-proc). Windows has no load average: load1 / load5 / load15 are null there, not 0 (0 would read as an idle machine).

memory:observed.description: Memory and swap in KiB (rheon-proc). used_kb is total minus available.

cpu:observed.description: Usage of one CPU core over a 0.2 s sample (rheon-proc); one record per core. The slow kind.

disk:observed.description: One mounted filesystem in KiB (rheon-proc), like df. Filesystems with a size of 0 are left out.

netif:observed.description: Counters of one network interface since boot (rheon-proc); sorted by name.

pipe:installed.description: One installed pipe, as `rheon list --json` reports it: what its declaration says it is, where it sits in a pipeline, and what the binary on the shelf answers.

bin_name.description: What you type. Equal to id by convention.

category.description: Where it sits: source / filter / sink. Empty when the declaration names none.

verbs.description: Dot-chain shell verb names. Empty is a normal shape (a CLI with no dot-verb).

version.description: The semver the binary itself names; null when it names none (Python tools) or is missing.

build_id.description: The build id the binary names.

path.description: Where the binary should be on the shelf.

reachable.description: Whether PATH resolves the name to that binary.

state.description: missing: declared but no binary; shadowed: another binary answers to the name first; torn: the declaration disagrees with the binary. null when none.

detail.description: For shadowed / torn: the other path, or both versions.

time:observed.description: The current time, and where the time zone came from, as rheon-time emits it -- date for records. tz_source exists because date cannot say whether the zone came from TZ or from the OS setting; a missing TZ silently makes a producer cut its days in UTC.

utc.description: ISO 8601 in UTC, ending in Z (microseconds when not zero).

local.description: ISO 8601 in the local zone, with its offset.

tz.description: The IANA zone name, or null when it cannot be named -- never guessed (an empty TZ is UTC to libc, but its name is null).

abbr.description: What the OS calls the zone now (JST, EDT; a display name on Windows). Not a substitute for tz.

tz_source.description: Where the zone name came from: the TZ variable, or the OS setting. null when neither named it.

tz_env.description: The TZ variable as is: null when unset, "" when set and empty (kept apart).

tally:observed.description: One group of records and how many there were, as rheon-count emits it: sort | uniq -c for records. The grouped value sits under the grouped field's own name (`by`), or under `value` when that name is one of this record's own fields. Not count:observed -- rheon-wc uses that name with other fields.

by.description: The field the records were grouped by.

count.description: How many records had this value.

value.description: The grouped value, when the grouped field's name collides with this record's own fields (v / source / type / event / by / count / ts).

additionalProperties.description: The grouped value, under the grouped field's own name (`by`). null groups the records that lacked the field.

pipeline:accepted.description: `hsh --check-flux-pipe` accepted the pipeline: only declared pipes (and sig / unsig) joined by `|`, with plain arguments. A runner asks this before running it.

name.description: The command name of the stage.

args.description: How many arguments it was given.

pipeline:refused.description: `hsh --check-flux-pipe` refused the pipeline, saying which stage and why.

stage.description: 1-based stage number; null when the shape of the whole pipeline is the problem.

reason.description: A short machine word: not-declared / writes / redirect / variable / command-substitution / not-one-pipeline / no-declarations / ...

detail.description: One sentence for a person or an agent to act on.

priority:scored.description: A record from upstream with a score and rank attached (rheon-priority): the upstream record is kept whole in payload, and original_type / original_source name it. Results come highest score first.

path.description: The file the wrapped record points to — a copy of payload.path, so a downstream tool that reads a record's path follows it.

is_dir.description: A copy of payload.is_dir, present when the wrapped record says it.

reasons.description: What the score is made of: factor / weight / value / detail.

bookkeeping.description: log / lockfile -- present only when it applies

var:observed.description: One variable, as it was when observed. rheon-env reports the process environment -- what a child process receives; flux-set (an hsh builtin) reports the shell's own variables, exported or not, in the order set lists them. value null means the value was withheld (redacted), never an empty or missing value.

value.description: The raw value. For an array (flux-set), the spelling set uses, e.g. ([0]="a" [1]="b"); its contents are in elements. null only when redacted.

shape.description: Both producers write it: rheon-env always scalar, since an environment variable has no arrays.

elements.description: flux-set, arrays only: an indexed array's values in index order (an array), or an associative array's pairs (an object). Absent when redacted.

indices.description: flux-set: the indices of a sparse indexed array (absent when they are 0..n-1).

attrs.description: Both producers write it. flux-set: exported, readonly, integer, nameref, uppercase, lowercase, capitalize. rheon-env: always ["exported"] -- what a child receives is exported by definition.

list.description: A PATH-like value split into its entries; null for other variables and when redacted.

origin.description: rheon-env on Windows: where the variable is defined (user, system, user+system, process); null elsewhere.

redacted.description: The name says the value is a secret (TOKEN, SECRET, KEY as a word, ...) and --reveal was not given.

function:observed.description: One shell function, as it was when observed (flux-set, an hsh builtin). Not emitted in sh mode (hsh --sh), where set lists variables only.

body.description: The definition as declare -f and set print it (name () { ... }).

expansion:resolved.description: A parameter expansion the shell resolved (hsh journal). Off by default: written only when HSH_JOURNAL_EXPANSION is set.

disk:sampled.description: Free space of one fixed disk, sampled every 5 minutes by a Windows system monitor's disk provider into its daily journal, so it carries ts. Readers fit a slope over the last 24 h to say how fast the disk is filling and when it runs out.

ts.description: RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. When the sample was taken, by the producer's clock (§2.05).

mount.description: Mount point as the OS names it (on Windows the drive root, e.g. "C:\\"). One record per fixed disk per sample; removable and network drives are not sampled.

total_bytes.description: Capacity of the volume in bytes.

free_bytes.description: Space available to the user in bytes. Raw bytes on purpose: rate, days left and thresholds are the reader's job, not stored.

memory:sampled.description: Commit charge and physical memory of a Windows machine, from one GetPerformanceInfo call (a Windows system monitor's memory provider). Read every 2 s and recorded every 5 minutes with the highest commit seen in between, so a short spike between two records is still in the journal. Stored, so it carries ts.

ts.description: RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. When the record was written, by the producer's clock (§2.05).

commit_bytes.description: Commit charge at ts (CommitTotal x PageSize).

commit_peak_bytes.description: Highest commit charge seen since the previous memory:sampled record (read every 2 s). Not the system-wide CommitPeak since boot: it starts over at every record, which places a spike in time.

commit_limit_bytes.description: Commit limit at ts (RAM plus page files; it moves when a page file grows). Reaching it is what fails an allocation with os error 1455 while physical memory may still look free.

physical_total_bytes.description: Installed physical memory visible to the OS.

reveal:navigated-away.description: One line from Marrow's worker log where a reveal loop (or the crawler's one-shot click) decided the page had become a different document and stopped. Collected from the container log, which is lost on rotation and on every redeploy. Stored, so it carries ts.

ts.description: RFC 3339. The time docker stamped on the log line (the worker's clock), not when it was collected.

container.description: Short container id the line came from. A redeploy starts a new container and a new log.

commit.description: The commit the worker image was built from, as /health named it at collection time. null when /health did not say.

source.description: Which layer logged it: reveal (inside revealLoop) or crawler (Marrow's restore, which follows a reveal stop or judges its own one-shot click).

by.description: What judged the move, as the producer named it (e.g. deep, both, url). Not a closed set; it may grow. null when the line could not be parsed.

from.description: URL before the click, as logged (the worker logs the address without the fragment).

to.description: URL after the click, as logged.

fixture.description: True when the URL is the deploy check's own fixture server, i.e. not a customer read. Kept so the deploy check's path is visible too.

line.description: The raw log line, so a parse that went wrong can be redone.

page:opened.description: A page was opened in a new session (browse_open / hand_open). Producers: marrow-browse (its own Chrome) and a browser extension (the person's Chrome); `source` says which. The journal stays local: page bodies, typed text and query values are never written; control labels are kept whole.

ts.description: RFC 3339. When the producer wrote the record (the MCP server's clock).

session.description: The producer's session id (marrow-browse s_…, the browser extension h_…). Not hsh's sid and not berthd's session — see session:* / attach:*.

url.description: What was ASKED for, redacted (the browser extension) or where the open landed (marrow-browse).

url_after.description: Where it landed, only when different from url (a redirect or a wall).

ok.description: false when the page could not be opened at all.

arrival.description: How far the first map can be trusted: stable / quiet / cap / unwatched / unreadable (marrow-browse).

arrival_ms.description: How long the arrival watch ran.

affordances.description: How many controls the first map listed.

sign_in_required.description: true when the page carried the site's own sign-in field (autocomplete=current-password) when the record was written; "unreadable" when it could not be checked; absent when checked and none. A fact about the page — a person being called is handoff:*.

knocks.description: The browser extension: extension sightings when not connected.

attachments.description: The browser extension: extension attachments seen.
